cases.prompt: Some people believe public transport should be free in large cities. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
cases.essay: I largely agree that cities should subsidise public transport because lower fares can reduce private-car use. However, a small charge may still be needed to maintain reliable services.

cases.prompt: Some people think children should begin formal education very early, while others prefer a later start. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
cases.essay: An early start can provide structure, whereas a later start leaves more time for play. In my view, formal lessons should begin later because young children learn effectively through guided play.

cases.prompt: Do the advantages of remote work outweigh the disadvantages?
cases.essay: Remote work saves commuting time but can weaken informal collaboration. The time and flexibility gained generally outweigh this drawback when teams have deliberate communication routines.

cases.prompt: What problems are caused by excessive packaging, and what measures can businesses take to address them?
cases.essay: Excessive packaging increases landfill waste and transport emissions. Businesses can reduce these effects by standardising reusable containers and removing unnecessary layers.

cases.prompt: Why are fewer young people learning to cook? Is this a positive or negative development?
cases.essay: Many young adults rely on convenient prepared food because they work long hours. This is mostly negative, since a lack of cooking skills can increase costs and reduce control over nutrition.

cases.prompt: Some people think museums should be free. Do you agree or disagree?
cases.essay: I agree. Museums are good and people can learn many things there. Therefore they should be free.

cases.prompt: The line graph shows average daily water consumption in two cities between 2000 and 2020.
cases.essay: Overall, consumption rose in both cities, and City A remained the larger user throughout. City A increased from 120 to 160 litres, while City B rose from 80 to 130 litres.

facts.statement: City A increased from 120 to 160 litres per person.
City B increased from 80 to 130 litres per person.

cases.prompt: The bar chart compares recycling rates for paper, glass and plastic in 2010 and 2020.
cases.essay: Plastic had the highest recycling rate in both years, reaching 90 percent in 2020. Paper changed very little over the period.

visualFacts.title: Recycling rates by material
keyFeatures: Paper was highest in both years

facts.statement: Paper rose from 70 percent to 80 percent.
Plastic rose from 20 percent to 35 percent.

cases.prompt: The diagram illustrates how used glass bottles are recycled.
cases.essay: Overall, bottle recycling is a circular process with collection, cleaning and remanufacturing stages. Used bottles are collected, sorted by colour, washed, crushed and melted before new bottles are formed.

visualFacts.title: Glass bottle recycling
keyFeatures: New bottles return to use after remanufacturing

facts.statement: Bottles are sorted by colour before washing.
Crushed glass is melted before new bottles are formed.

cases.essay: Housing accounted for exactly 47.3 percent of spending, while transport represented 18.6 percent.
